1a: 2. Definitions and preliminary considerations. A directed linear graph \(G(V,E)\) (or simply digraph G) consists of a set \(V\) of elements called nodes together with a set \(E\) of ordered pairs of the form \((i,j)\), \(i\) and \(j\in V\), called the directed edges (or simply edges) of the digraph; the node \(i\) is called the initial node and node \(j\) the terminal node. Together they are called the endpoints of the edge \((i,j)\).

For any \(i\in V\) the symbols \(\rho(i)\) and \(\rho^*(i)\) denote the cardinals of the sets of edges of \(G\) having \(i\) as initial and terminal nodes, respectively. They are called the outgoing and incoming degrees of \(G\) at \(i\). A digraph is regular of degree k if \(\rho(i)=\rho^*(i)=k\) for each \(i\in V\). A digraph is symmetric if it has the property that if \((i,j)\in E\), then \((j,i)\in E\).
A digraph \(S\) is a subgraph of \(G\) if the nodes and edges of \(S\) are nodes and
1b: edges respectively of \(G\) and if each edge of \(S\) has the same initial node and the same terminal node in \(S\) as in \(G\). If the node set and the edge set of \(S\) are both empty, then \(S\) is called the empty graph \(\varnothing\) of \(G\). A node not incident to any edge is called an isolated node. A digraph consisting only of isolated nodes is called the null graph. The empty graph is considered as a subgraph of every digraph. A directed circuit of \(G\) is a connected regular subgraph of degree 1. Two subgraphs are disjoint when they have no nodes in common. If \(S\) is a subgraph of \(G\) and each node of \(G\) is a node of \(S\), then \(S\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\). A directed path \(P_{ij}\) is a sequence of the form \(P_{ij}=(i,k_1)(k_1,k_2)(k_2,k_3)\cdots(k_m,j)\in E\) where \(i,j,\) and \(k_t,\ t=1,\cdots,m,\) are nodes in \(V\). It is not required that all the nodes of \(P_{ij}\) shall be distinct. If they are, \(P_{ij}\) is said to be a directed simple path. Again node \(i\) is called the initial node of \(P_{ij}\) and node \(j\) the terminal node. Both nodes \(i\) and \(j\) are referred to as end nodes. A directed circuit (or a directed path) is of length m if the number of edges contained in the directed circuit (directed path) is \(m\).
1c: If the order of two endpoints of an edge is immaterial, i.e., \((i,j)=(j,i)\), then the edge is called an undirected edge. An undirected graph is a graph in which every edge is undirected. To every directed graph \(G(V,E)\), there is also a corresponding undirected graph \(G_u(V_u,E_u)\) (or simply \(G_u\)) such that \(V_u=V\) and \((i,j)=(j,i)\in E_u\) if either \((i,j)\in E\) or \((j,i)\in E\) or both. Usually, a digraph \(G\) can be represented equivalently by a geometric diagram: The nodes are indicated by small circles, while any two of them, \(i\) and \(j\), are joined by an arrowheaded continuous curve, or even a straight line, from \(i\) to \(j\) if \((i,j)\in E\). Similarly, an undirected graph can also be represented equivalently by a geometric diagram such that there is a continuous curve from \(i\) to \(j\) if \((i,j)=(j,i)\in E_u\). More intuitively \(G_u\) of \(G\) can be obtained from \(G\) by omitting the arrowheads and combining the parallel curves. The geometric concept may be considered slightly general since each curve may be counted with a certain multiplicity. This will be excluded in this discussion. However, all the results obtained here can be extended easily, and the extension is almost trivial.

Sometimes, it is desirable to change an undirected graph \(G_u\) into a directed one \(G\) by the process of duplication: one replaces each undirected edge in \(G_u\) by two edges with the same endpoints; to the two edges in such a pair one assigns opposite orders (or directions). An undirected path \(P_{ij}\) of \(G_u\) is a sequence of undirected edges of \(G_u\) which has the same form as defined earlier for a directed path. \(G\) is said to be connected if, for any two nodes \(i\) and \(j\), there exists an undirected path in \(G_u\) with these two nodes as end nodes. A component of \(G\) is a maximal connected subgraph of \(G\). Let \(A\) be a subset of \(V\); then the sectional graph \(G[A]\) of \(G\) defined by \(A\) is the subgraph
1d: whose node set is \(A\) and whose edges are all those edges in \(G\) which connect two nodes in \(A\).

A tree t of \(G_u\) is a spanning subgraph which is connected and contains no undirected circuits. A spanning subgraph \(H\) of \(G_u\) is said to be a k-tree of \(G_u\) if \(H\) has \(k\) components and contains no undirected circuits. Some of the components may each consist of an isolated node. Very often, \(k\)-trees in which certain designated nodes are required to be in different components are used. For example, \(t_{ab,cde,f}\) is the symbol for a 3-tree in which the nodes \(a,b\) are in one component, the nodes \(c,d,e\) in one component, and the node \(f\) in one component. A subgraph, denoted by \(t^r\), of a digraph \(G(V,E)\) is said to be a directed tree if and only if (1) the corresponding undirected graph of \(t^r\) forms a tree in the corresponding undirected graph \(G_u\) of \(G\); and (2) \(\rho(i)=1\) for all \(i\in V-r\) where \(r\) is called the reference node of \(G\) and \(V-r\) is the node set with node \(r\) having been deleted from \(V\), and \(\rho(r)=0\). A subgraph, denoted by \(t^r_{r,i}\), of \(G\) is said to be a directed 2-tree if and only if (1) the corresponding undirected graph of \(t^r_{r,i}\) is a 2-tree in the corresponding undirected graph \(G_u\) of \(G\); (2) each of the two components of \(t^r_{r,i}\) is a directed tree for some sectional graph of \(G\); node \(r\) serves as a reference node for one of such directed trees; and node \(i\) for the other. The extension to directed k-tree is obvious. Again \(t^r_{ra,jbc,k}\) is the symbol for a directed 3-tree in which the nodes \(r,a\) are in one component; the nodes \(j,b,c\) in one component; and the node \(k\) in one component. Nodes \(r,j,k\) are the reference nodes of the components.
1f: For a given set \(A\), \(\mu(A)\) is used to denote the number of elements in \(A\). For convenience, edges of a given digraph \(G(V,E)\) will also be represented by letters \(e_i\). Each subgraph \(Q\) of \(G\) may be expressed by the “product” or by juxtaposition of its elements provided that \(Q\) contains no isolated nodes; i.e., for example, a directed tree may be represented by \(e_{i_1}e_{i_2}\cdots e_{i_{\mu(V)-1}}\). Two set-theoretic binary operations, “union” and “intersection” represented by \(\cup\) and \(\cap\), respectively, will be used. \(g_1\cup g_2\) is a subgraph of \(G\) consisting of all elements which are either in \(g_1\) or in \(g_2\) or in both, where \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) are two subgraphs of \(G\). \(g_1\cap g_2\) is a subgraph consisting of all elements which are in both \(g_1\) and \(g_2\). Again if \(g_1\cup g_2\) contains no isolated nodes, then it may be represented by the product of its elements. Similarly for \(g_1\cap g_2\); i.e., for example, if \(g_1=e_1e_2e_3e_4\) and \(g_2=e_1e_4e_5e_6\), then \(g_1\cup g_2=e_1e_2e_3e_4e_5e_6\) and \(g_1\cap g_2=e_1e_4\).
2a: 3. Proposed algebra. Let \(D\) be the set of all subgraphs of a given digraph \(G(V,E)\). Consider the set \(H\) of all subsets of \(D\) for which an equivalence relation “\(=\)” is defined. Assume in \(H\) there are two binary operations. One of these binary operations is called the “ring-sum” and is denoted by the symbol \(\oplus\). The second of these operations is called “star” and is denoted
2b: by the symbol \(*\). These two operations are defined to satisfy the following rules: for \(h_1,h_2\in H\),
\[h_1\oplus h_2=\{x\mid x\text{ is in }h_1,\text{ or in }h_2,\text{ but not in both}\},\]
\[h_1*h_2=\{x\cup y\mid x\in h_1,\ y\in h_2,\text{ and }x\cap y=\varnothing\}.\]

It can easily be shown that the operations defined here are commutative and associative. Furthermore, the set \(H\) forms an abelian group with respect to the ring-sum operation, and a commutative semigroup with unity with respect to the star operation. The zero element in \(H\) is the empty set of \(H\) and is denoted by \(h_0=\{\ \}\), while the identity element is \(\{\varnothing\}\), where \(\varnothing\) is the empty graph of \(G\). For every \(h\in H\), \(h_0*h\) is defined to be \(h_0\); and the inverse of \(h\) relative to the ring-sum operation is itself, i.e., \(h\oplus h=h_0\).
3a: (a) For symmetrical digraphs. Assume that the given digraph \(G(V,E)\) is symmetric, and all the nodes of \(V\) are labelled by one of the integers from 1 to \(\mu(V)\). Let \(C_1\) be the Cartesian product of the subsets \(S_k\), i.e.,

where \(S_k=\{(k,t)\mid(k,t)\in E\text{ and }t=1,2,\cdots,k-1,k+1,\cdots,\mu(V)\}\) for \(k=1,2,\cdots,\mu(V)\), and \(k\ne r\), where \(r\) is an arbitrary node of \(V\). Thus \(C_1\) is the set of all subgraphs of \(G\) with outgoing degree 1 except at \(r\) where it is 0. It follows that the set of elements of \(C_1\) can in general be grouped into three disjoint subsets \(M_t,\ t=1,2,3,\) such that
\[M_1=\{c_i\mid c_i\in C_1,\text{ and }c_i\text{ is a directed tree of }G\},\]
\[M_2=\{c_i\mid c_i\in C_1,\text{ and there exists at least one directed circuit of length 2 in }c_i\},\]
\[M_3=\{c_i\mid c_i\in C_1,\text{ and }c_i\text{ is not a directed tree of }G\text{ and contains no directed circuits of length 2}\}.\]

Since there exists a one-to-one correspondence between directed trees of a symmetrical digraph \(G\) and trees of the corresponding undirected graph \(G_u\) of \(G\), [7], it is simpler to consider \(G_u\) rather than \(G\), i.e., one considers \((i,j)=(j,i)\) for all \((i,j)\in E\). Consequently:
3b: THEOREM 1. In a given symmetric digraph \(G(V,E)\), let \(X_1=S_1*S_2*\cdots*S_{r-1}*S_{r+1}*\cdots*S_{\mu(V)}\), where \(S_k=\{(k,t)\mid(k,t)\in E\text{ and }t=1,2,\cdots,k-1,k+1,\cdots,\mu(V)\}\) for \(k=1,2,\cdots,r-1,r+1,\cdots,\mu(V)\), and \(r\in V\) is the reference node of \(G\). Also let \(T^r=\{x_1\}\oplus\{x_2\}\oplus\cdots\oplus\{x_{\mu(X_1)}\}\), where \(x_i\in X_1\) for \(i=1,2,\cdots,\mu(X_1)\). Then the set of all distinct directed trees \(t^r\) of \(G(V,E)\) is given by \(T^r\) provided \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) are considered identical in the operations.
Proof. By Lemma 1 it is apparent that \(X_1\) is the set union of \(M_1\) and \(M_3\). By Lemma 2 it follows that \(M_1=T^r\). This completes the proof of the theorem.
